title: I Am A Sixty Eight Year Old Retired School Bus Driver Who Drives For A Ride App, And When A Shaking Elderly Woman Climbed Into My Back Seat With A Thick Envelope While A Man On Her Phone Coached Her On What To Tell The Bank Teller About Her
excerpt: I’ve been driving for a ride app for three years. Most rides are boring. Airports. Bars. Grocery stores. Hospital discharges. College kids who fall asleep in the back seat and have to be woken up at their dorm.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — BORING RIDES

I’ve been driving for a ride app for three years. Most rides are boring. Airports. Bars. Grocery stores. Hospital discharges. College kids who fall asleep in the back seat and have to be woken up at their dorm.

I’m sixty-eight. My name is Earl. Before this, I drove a yellow school bus in Tucson, Arizona, for twenty-seven years. Route 14, mostly. Elementary kids in the morning, middle schoolers in the afternoon. I knew every kid by name and every dog on the route by bark. When I retired, the kids made me a card shaped like a bus. It’s still on my refrigerator.

I started driving for the app because retirement was too quiet. My wife, Darlene, says I need people the way some men need coffee. She’s not wrong. I like talking to folks. I like getting them where they need to go.

Driving a school bus for twenty-seven years teaches you some things. You learn to look in the big mirror every few seconds. You learn to tell the difference between a kid who’s being silly and a kid who’s scared. You learn that the quiet ones are usually the ones who need you most.
Last Tuesday, around ten in the morning, I got a ride request from a senior apartment complex on the east side. The pickup name was “Margaret.”

She was waiting by the curb with a walker. Maybe eighty. White hair, a lavender raincoat even though it wasn’t raining, and big glasses. She had a cell phone pressed to her ear and a thick envelope clutched in her lap once I helped her into the back seat.
I put her walker in the trunk. When I got back in, she was still on the phone. She covered it with her hand.
“I need to go to my bank first,” she said. “On Broadway. And then to a shipping store. Please hurry. It’s an emergency.”
The quiet ones are usually the ones who need you most.
PART 2 — THE VOICE ON THE PHONE
I pulled out of the lot. Like I said, I’ve been doing this three years, and I mind my own business. Passengers make phone calls. It’s not my concern.
But the car is small and the phone was loud. I could hear a man’s voice on the other end. Young-ish. Fast. Bossy.

“Okay, Margaret, listen carefully,” he said. “When you get to the bank, you go to the teller. You withdraw the money in cash. If they ask what it’s for, remember, it’s for your grandson’s car. Say you’re helping him buy a car. Don’t say anything else. Do you understand?”
“Yes,” she whispered. “His car. I understand.”
“And don’t tell anybody about Tyler. Remember what the lawyer said. There’s a gag order. If you tell anyone, it could make things worse for him.”

I’m not a cop. I’m a retired school bus driver. But I’ve seen the news. I’ve seen the flyers at the senior center where Darlene plays cards. I know about these scams. Somebody calls an old person pretending to be a grandchild in trouble, or a lawyer for the grandchild. The grandchild has been arrested, or in a car accident, and needs money for bail or a lawyer. Don’t tell anyone. It has to be cash. It has to be now.
And the shipping store. That was the part that made the hair on my arms stand up. Who sends bail money through a shipping store?
I looked in the mirror again. Margaret was holding the envelope with both hands, so tight her knuckles were white. Her lips were moving, like she was praying.
Twenty-seven years of looking in that big mirror, and I knew that look. It was the look of a scared kid who doesn’t know who to tell.
Who sends bail money through a shipping store?
PART 3 — ONE STOP FIRST
I could have just driven to the bank. That’s my job. Pick up, drop off, five stars, next ride. The app doesn’t pay me to ask questions. Honestly, the app would probably prefer I didn’t.

But I kept thinking about those kids on Route 14. The ones who wouldn’t tell their parents something was wrong. The ones who got off the bus slower than the others. Sometimes all they needed was one grown-up to ask.
The man on the phone finally said he’d call back in five minutes, when she got to the bank. Margaret lowered the phone into her lap, next to the envelope.
I kept my voice easy and slow, like I used to talk to the little ones.
“Ma’am,” I said, “is everything all right? You seem worried.”

“My grandson is in jail,” she said, and her voice cracked right in half. “He was in a car accident. He hit a woman. She’s pregnant. They arrested him. He needs bail money. Eight thousand dollars. The lawyer said I can’t tell anyone or the judge will be angry.”

I had driven a Tyler Briggs on Route 14. Little kid with red hair and a Spider-Man backpack. He used to sit right behind me and tell me knock-knock jokes, every morning, for three years. His grandmother used to wait for him at the bus stop in a lavender raincoat.
I looked in the mirror again, and this time I really looked.
“Ma’am,” I said, “would you mind if I made one stop first?”
She hesitated. She looked out the window. Then she looked back at me in the mirror, and something in her face loosened, just a little.
His grandmother used to wait for him at the bus stop in a lavender raincoat.
PART 4 — THE POLICE STATION
There’s a police substation two blocks from the bank on Broadway. I’ve driven past it a thousand times. I pulled into the lot and parked right by the door.
Margaret looked confused. “This isn’t the bank.”
“No, ma’am,” I said. “I’d just like somebody to double-check things for you. Before you spend Tyler’s eight thousand dollars. Would that be all right?”
She looked at the building. Her lip trembled. “He said not to tell anyone,” she whispered.
“I know he did,” I said. “That’s exactly why I think we should.”

I got her walker out of the trunk and walked her inside, slowly, one step at a time. The officer at the front desk was a young guy, maybe thirty, with a buzz cut. I told him, quietly, that I thought this lady might be the victim of a grandparent scam and that she was carrying a lot of cash.
He took one look at the thick envelope in her hands. He didn’t need me to explain anything else.
He came around the desk and pulled out a chair for her. He got her a paper cup of water. He was kind. He said his own grandmother had gotten a call like this once.
Right then, her phone rang. Same number. The man calling back.
The officer held out his hand. “Ma’am, may I?”
“Margaret? Margaret, are you at the bank? Did you get the money?”
The officer said, in a calm, flat voice, “This is Officer Ruiz with the Tucson Police Department. Who is this?”
This is Officer Ruiz with the Tucson Police Department. Who is this?
PART 5 — TYLER
Margaret stared at the phone in the officer’s hand like it had bitten her.
“Yes, ma’am,” Officer Ruiz said gently. “Real lawyers don’t hang up on police officers.”
Then she started to cry. Not loud. Just quiet tears running down behind those big glasses. I sat next to her and she grabbed my hand and didn’t let go.
“But Tyler,” she said. “Where is Tyler? Is he hurt?”

Officer Ruiz asked if she had Tyler’s real phone number. She did. It was written on an index card in her purse, in big letters, with all her grandchildren’s numbers. The scammer had told her not to call it, because Tyler’s phone had been “taken as evidence.”
The officer dialed it on his own desk phone and put it on speaker.
It rang twice. Then a young man’s voice. “Hello? This is Tyler.”
“Tyler,” the officer said, “this is the Tucson Police Department. You’re not in any trouble. I’m here with your grandmother. Can you tell me where you are right now?”
“I’m at work,” Tyler said, totally confused. “At the bike shop. Is Grandma okay?”
Margaret let out a sound I’ll never forget. Half a sob and half a laugh. She grabbed the phone right off the desk with both hands.
